authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro (candidate author; not a human reviewer)

items.prompt: Select all boundary contracts that preserve the stated meaning on an empty tree.

options.text: A whole-tree sum returns `0`.
A whole-tree maximum returns an explicit no-result value such as `None` or an empty optional.
A whole-tree maximum always returns `0`.
A whole-tree node count returns `1` for the missing root.

feedback.reason: Empty input uses the identity of the requested operation when one exists; otherwise the API must represent absence rather than invent a value.

blocks.text: Addition has a neutral element, so zero is the natural sum of no nodes. Maximum over an empty set has no ordinary numeric value unless the domain and contract supply a safe sentinel, so an optional result states the absence precisely. Returning zero for maximum fails when all legal values are negative and confuses a real value with no result. Counting a missing root as one invents a node. Boundary behavior belongs to each query's output contract, not to a universal “null means zero” rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.maximum_is_zero: Zero is plausible as a familiar default, but it may exceed every actual negative value and is a valid payload. It is safe only when the value domain and API explicitly declare zero as a sentinel outside all legal results.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.size_is_one: A null root represents zero nodes. Returning one would fit a different measure such as counting an external null marker, not node count.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sum_is_zero: Without the additive identity, callers need unnecessary special cases and a leaf recurrence will not compose cleanly.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.maximum_is_absent: Without an absence representation, the function must fabricate a maximum for a set with no elements.

constraints: Node values may be negative, zero, or positive.
The API may use an optional result type.

items.prompt: Under the standard binary-tree node contract used throughout this batch, which description correctly identifies a leaf node?

options.text: A non-null node whose left and right child references are both null.
Any non-null node with at least one null child.
The null reference reached after stepping past a node.
Whichever node happens to be deepest in the current DFS branch.

feedback.reason: A leaf is an actual node with no children; a unary node remains internal, and null is missing structure rather than a node.

blocks.text: The definition is structural and independent of traversal history. A node with only one child still has a descendant and is not terminal. Null calls are useful base cases but do not become leaves. “Deepest seen” is an observation relative to one traversal and can change when another branch is explored. This boundary controls root-to-leaf path completion, leaf counts, and algorithms that apply work only at terminal nodes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.at_least_one_missing: This is a common shortcut that wrongly classifies unary nodes as leaves. It becomes valid only under a nonstandard contract that defines terminality by a missing designated edge.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.null_reference: Null marks the absence of a node. Some edge-based recurrences process null markers, but they must not call those markers leaves without redefining the model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.deepest_seen: Depth does not define leaf status; an internal node can be deeper than a leaf in another branch. This could identify a current traversal maximum, not a structural category.

items.prompt: A tree contains exactly one node with value `8`. Which statement about its standard traversals is correct?

options.text: Preorder, inorder, and postorder all emit `[8]`, while level order emits one level containing `8`.
Only preorder emits the node because the other traversals require children.
Because the orders agree here, traversal order is irrelevant for every tree.
Level order returns no levels because the root has no children.

feedback.reason: With no child operations to interleave, all DFS action positions collapse to the same one-node sequence, but that boundary case does not erase their differences on larger trees.

blocks.text: Each standard traversal processes every real node once. On a singleton, the left and right subtree calls are empty, so placing the current action before, between, or after them yields the same visible value. BFS has a nonempty root frontier and therefore one level. This is a useful test boundary because an implementation can pass it while still ordering larger trees incorrectly; tests must include a node with both child structure and observable ordering.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.preorder_only: Inorder and postorder do not require non-null children; their empty child calls simply contribute no values. All three still process the current node.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.orders_are_globally_equivalent: Agreement on a degenerate input does not prove semantic equivalence. The orders diverge as soon as child and parent actions can be interleaved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_empty: A root is itself a level even when it has no children. Empty level order applies only to a null root.

constraints: All traversals visit actual nodes and omit null markers.

items.prompt: A recursive DFS is linear-time on every proper tree. What additional boundary must be considered for a tree shaped as a chain of `n` nodes?

options.text: The recursion depth becomes `n`, so auxiliary stack use is `O(n)` and may exceed the runtime's call-stack limit.
The traversal becomes exponential because every node has one child.
Moving the output to a global list makes recursion depth constant.
Adding a visited set reduces the recursion depth to `O(log n)`.

feedback.reason: Linear node visits do not bound recursion depth; a skewed tree has height `n` and keeps one frame per node on the active path.

blocks.text: Tree shape controls `h`, the maximum live recursive chain. A balanced tree has logarithmic height, but a chain has `h = n`, so a correct `O(n)` DFS can still overflow a bounded language stack. An explicit stack moves storage to the heap but remains `O(n)` for the chain. Global output state and visited state do not change structural height. The practical boundary may motivate an iterative implementation even when asymptotic time is already optimal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_exponential: Each node still has only one recursive child call and is visited once, so time remains linear. Exponential growth requires repeated branching or recomputation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_list_fixes_depth: Output location does not remove active recursive calls or shorten the root-to-leaf chain. It can change state ownership, but the call-stack depth remains proportional to tree height.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_set_balances_tree: Visited state prevents revisits in graphs; it does not change the tree's shape or execution path length.

constraints: Each node is visited exactly once.
The language runtime has a finite call-stack limit.

items.prompt: A proper binary tree contains two different nodes whose values are both `4`. Which traversal policy preserves the tree correctly?

options.text: Visit both nodes; equal payload values do not merge their identities.
Treat the second `4` as already visited and skip its subtree.
Combine the two nodes into one logical node because their values match.
Use a value-based visited set, as graph DFS would.

feedback.reason: Tree nodes are structural identities, while values are payload; duplicate values remain separate positions and must both be traversed.

blocks.text: A proper tree already guarantees one structural route to each node, so no visited set is needed. Even when a graph requires visited state, it is normally keyed by vertex identity, not payload value. Skipping or merging equal values changes node count, topology, and any subtree below the skipped node. Value-based deduplication is valid only when the problem explicitly defines values as unique identifiers and duplicates as aliases, which is not the standard tree contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_second_value: This confuses equality with identity and loses a real node and its descendants. It is valid only under an explicit deduplication-by-key data model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.merge_subtrees: Equal payloads do not imply equal child structure or ownership. Merging mutates the represented tree into another graph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.add_graph_visited_by_value: Graph traversal uses identity-based discovery because values may repeat. Adding a value-based set imports the wrong graph rule and is unnecessary for a proper tree.

constraints: Node values are not unique identifiers.
The input satisfies proper-tree structure.

items.prompt: A recursive tree helper must distinguish an empty subtree from a leaf. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Null means no node and uses the operation's identity; a leaf is a real node whose two child results use that identity.
A leaf is equivalent to null because both have no non-null children.
Null should be processed as a node with a default payload before checking children.
Leaves can always be skipped because they contribute no child state.

feedback.reason: Empty structure and a real node with empty children have different semantic roles in a recursive contract.

blocks.text: A null call represents an empty region and returns the identity for the helper's combine operation. A leaf still contributes its own value, count, or node identity, then combines two identity child results. Treating the leaf as null drops valid data; treating null as a node invents a payload. Boundary handling must preserve the public meaning of both cases.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.leaf_is_null: A leaf is present and contributes its node value or identity even though both child references are null.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.null_is_node: Null has no payload and should terminate before node-specific processing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_leaf: Leaves are often the base contributors for subtree aggregates, so skipping them changes the result.

constraints: The helper's result is defined for both null and non-null roots.

items.prompt: A single-node tree is processed by a subtree aggregate whose null-child identity is 0 and whose node contribution is 1. What result should the root return?

options.text: 1, because the root contributes one and both null children contribute zero.
0, because both child subtrees are empty.
2, because the root has two child references.
Undefined, because a single-node tree has no recursive descendants.

feedback.reason: A leaf is a real subtree containing one node; null children contribute only their identity.

blocks.text: The recurrence is contribution(node) + aggregate(left) + aggregate(right). For a leaf this becomes 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. The number of child references is structural metadata, not node count, and the absence of descendants does not make the root absent. Testing a single-node tree exposes many off-by-one and null-identity errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Zero is the identity for each missing child, not the aggregate for the existing root.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two: Null references do not count as nodes; the child count is not the aggregate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.undefined: The recursive contract explicitly defines null children, so a leaf has a valid result.

constraints: The aggregate counts actual nodes and uses zero for an empty subtree.

items.prompt: Two distinct tree nodes contain the same value. A traversal must count nodes and preserve their structural positions. Which boundary rule applies?

options.text: Treat each node reference as a separate node; equal payload values do not justify deduplication.
Count one node per distinct value because duplicate payloads represent the same information.
Skip a right child when its value equals the parent to avoid repeated output.
Sort traversal output and remove duplicate values before counting.

feedback.reason: Tree traversal operates on node identity and edges unless the problem explicitly defines value-based deduplication.

blocks.text: A repeated value can occur at different structural positions and each node may have different children. Removing one by payload collapses distinct subtrees and changes counts, traversal output, and parent aggregates. A visited set is appropriate for shared graph references when the contract is per identity, but ordinary duplicate values in a proper tree are not repeated references.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dedupe_values: Equal payloads do not imply equal nodes or equal descendants.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_right_duplicate: Traversal order and node identity are independent of payload equality unless a duplicate policy explicitly says otherwise.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_unique: Sorting and deduplication change the requested structural traversal into a value-set operation.

constraints: The input is a proper tree and duplicate payload values are allowed.

items.prompt: A recursive traversal is correct on balanced examples but overflows the call stack on a chain of n nodes. What should the boundary audit record?

options.text: Auxiliary recursion space is O(h), which becomes O(n) for a skewed tree; the input shape is part of the operational contract.
Balanced examples prove the recursion uses O(log n) space for every valid tree.
Stack depth cannot affect correctness or resource safety because each node is visited once.
Remove repeated values from the chain; value uniqueness determines recursion depth.

feedback.reason: Recursion depth follows tree height, not node count's balanced-tree estimate.

blocks.text: A chain has height proportional to n, so one active call per ancestor can exhaust a fixed call stack even when time remains O(n). Balanced examples exercise only h = O(log n). The implementation should either state a height/resource precondition or use an explicit stack/iterative strategy if arbitrary valid shapes are allowed. Node values and duplicates do not determine structural depth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.balanced_only: Balance is a shape assumption, not a consequence of being a valid tree.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_only: A linear visit count does not bound the simultaneous call frames or prevent stack overflow.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dedupe_chain: Value deduplication would change data and does not reduce the number of structural edges in the chain.

constraints: The tree may be arbitrarily skewed and recursion stack is finite.

items.prompt: A helper returns the maximum value in a subtree, but the public contract allows an empty tree. Which design avoids confusing “no value” with a valid node value?

options.text: Return an explicit unavailable result such as an option/sentinel outside the value domain, or require a nonempty input contract.
Return zero for empty trees regardless of the allowed node-value range.
Use negative infinity without checking whether it belongs to the value domain or numeric type.
Return the first non-null child's maximum and ignore a lone root or other branch.

feedback.reason: An empty maximum has no ordinary value unless the API supplies a mathematically and representationally valid identity or absence marker.

blocks.text: Unlike sum or count, maximum has no universal identity inside every possible node-value domain. Zero may be a real value, and negative infinity may be unrepresentable or part of the domain. An option-like unavailable result or a precondition that the tree is nonempty makes the boundary explicit. The choice must be reflected in both the helper and its callers; silently inventing a value corrupts aggregates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_sentinel: Zero may be the true maximum of a nonempty tree, so it cannot generally encode absence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_infinity_always: The sentinel must be outside the allowed domain and supported by the numeric representation; that is not automatic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_child_only: A maximum helper must consider the current node and both subtrees according to its contract.

constraints: Node values may include zero and the tree may be empty.

items.prompt: Why must a recursive tree aggregate define a null-child identity explicitly?
constraints: Leaves invoke the helper on null children.
The parent combines child results algebraically.

options.text: The null result must be the correct identity or invalid marker for the parent recurrence, so leaf and unary cases are defined.
options.explanation: Base cases determine the recurrence's meaning.

options.text: Return zero for every aggregate because null contains no value.
options.explanation: Zero can be wrong for minimum, maximum, or existence semantics.

options.text: Skip null without initializing the missing child result.
options.explanation: The parent then combines undefined state.

options.text: Return the parent value for a null child to preserve the path.
options.explanation: A null child has no node value.

feedback.reason: Null is part of the mathematical contract of a subtree recurrence.

blocks.text: For count, zero may be the identity; for multiplication, one; for max or path existence, a special invalid state may be required. The parent formula must match the choice.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_always: Zero can be wrong for minimum, maximum, or existence semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_null: The parent then combines undefined state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.parent_copy: A null child has no node value.

items.prompt: What is the correct boundary interpretation for a single-node tree in a root-to-leaf query?
constraints: The root has no children.
The root's value contributes to the path.

options.text: The root is also a leaf, so the one-node path is a complete root-to-leaf path.
options.explanation: Leaf means no children, including the root.

options.text: There is no path because a path needs at least one edge.
options.explanation: A path may contain one vertex under the usual contract.

options.text: Only the null children count as leaves, not the root.
options.explanation: Null pointers are not data leaves.

options.text: Count the root once for itself and again for its null children.
options.explanation: The root belongs to the path exactly once.

feedback.reason: Short-tree boundaries should follow the structural definition of leaf.

blocks.text: A one-node tree is a valid root-to-leaf path of length one node. This case catches base logic that assumes an internal parent always exists.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_path: A path may contain one vertex under the usual contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.null_only: Null pointers are not data leaves.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.double_count: The root belongs to the path exactly once.

items.prompt: What does a skewed binary tree reveal about recursive tree algorithms?
constraints: Every node may have only one child.
The height can equal n.

options.text: It exposes recursion-depth and O(h) path-space risks and tests whether unary-child base cases are handled correctly.
options.explanation: A skewed tree is the worst shape for depth.

options.text: It is equivalent to a balanced tree because both contain n nodes.
options.explanation: Shape changes height and traversal memory.

options.text: It only tests BFS width because DFS has no shape-dependent cost.
options.explanation: DFS path depth is shape dependent.

options.text: Skewed trees must be sorted before any traversal can be correct.
options.explanation: Traversal correctness does not require sorting.

feedback.reason: Tree algorithms must state whether their cost depends on height, width, or both.

blocks.text: A chain-like tree makes h=n, so recursion can overflow and DFS stack can become linear. It also catches code that treats a missing left child as a leaf without checking a right child.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.balanced_assumed: Shape changes height and traversal memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.width_risk_only: DFS path depth is shape dependent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_needed: Traversal correctness does not require sorting.

items.prompt: Why should an empty tree result be distinguished from a node whose child pointer is null?
constraints: The output may describe nodes or subtree properties.
Null pointers are structural absence, not node records.

options.text: A null root means the entire tree is empty; a null child means only that one branch is absent and the parent still exists.
options.explanation: The two cases occur at different recursion levels.

options.text: Treat every null pointer as a separate empty tree in the final output.
options.explanation: That can emit many phantom trees or levels.

options.text: Emit null as a visited tree node whenever a child is absent.
options.explanation: Traversal normally visits actual nodes only.

options.text: Handle null root by creating a synthetic parent so child cases stay uniform.
options.explanation: Synthetic nodes can violate the output contract.

feedback.reason: Empty-root and missing-child semantics are related but not interchangeable.

blocks.text: The root-null case determines the whole result. During recursion, a null child supplies a base case to its existing parent. Confusing them creates phantom output or wrong aggregates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_output: That can emit many phantom trees or levels.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.null_node: Traversal normally visits actual nodes only.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_root: Synthetic nodes can violate the output contract.
